Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Clergy/Pastor
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Affective Expression: Crying, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Hopelessness: I have no future, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Vignette:
Preeti was forty-seven when she finally walked into a therapist’s office, but the woman who sat down across from the intake clinician was not the pastor her congregation had known for years. That version of Preeti—the one who could counsel a grieving widow at noon and lead a potluck supper by six, the one who believed brokenness could be redeemed—had been disappearing for months, and she had not known how to stop it.

The torture happened seventeen years ago, in a basement in the city where she had been born. She had been a lay preacher then, arrested for distributing tracts that the authorities considered seditious. There were four men. They wanted names. They did not believe her when she said she had no names to give. She remembered the fluorescent light overhead—that was clear, so clear she could still feel the buzz behind her eyes. But the rest came in pieces: the wet rope around her wrists, the smell of sweat and something metallic, the taste of something thick and salty that they forced into her mouth—she had never told anyone it tasted like a copper coin left on the tongue. She could not remember their faces, only the sound of one man’s belt buckle scraping against the cement floor. And then: blank. Hours missing. A different room. A woman’s voice saying something in a language Preeti did not understand. She had never been able to piece together how she got out.

For years she managed. She came to America as a refugee, completed seminary, took a pastorate in a midsized city. She worked hard. She did not talk about the basement. When well-meaning parishioners asked about her past, she smiled and said God had given her a second chance. She thought that was enough. But there had been one time, about three years ago, when she had tried. A young woman in the congregation, struggling with her own history of abuse, had asked Preeti how she had endured suffering without becoming bitter. Preeti had felt a sudden, unfamiliar urge to be honest. She had opened her mouth and said, “I was arrested once. They—” and then her chest had tightened, her vision had narrowed to a pinprick, and the fluorescent light of the church library had flickered into the basement’s hum. She had stopped talking mid-sentence, her hands shaking, her mouth filled with the taste of copper. The young woman had reached for her arm, but Preeti had pulled away, muttered an excuse about a meeting, and fled to her office. She had never tried to speak of it again. She told herself that sharing would only make it worse—that other people could not handle what had happened, and neither could she.

Lately, her body had begun to remember things her mind refused to. At the church’s monthly fellowship dinner, a volunteer served a lentil stew that tasted faintly of turmeric and something else—something metallic. Preeti did not even register the taste before her stomach clenched, her mouth went dry, and she was on her feet, excusing herself to the restroom, hands shaking. She stood over the sink and told herself she was safe. *You are in Ohio. The door is unlocked. The women’s auxiliary is two tables away.* But her body had already reacted: her heart pounding, her skin slick with cold sweat, before her mind had even caught up. She could not make herself believe the safety. Even when her associate pastor told her, gently, that there was nothing to fear, Preeti heard the words and felt nothing—no relief, only the certainty that the danger was still there, just out of sight.

She started scanning. Every new face in the sanctuary became a potential threat. A man in a dark coat sitting in the back row made her pulse jump. She found herself memorizing exits during sermons. She began to avoid the fellowship hall entirely, eating lunch alone in her office, chewing the same bland crackers every day, controlling every bite because the alternative—being caught off guard by a flavor—felt unbearable. She tried not to think about the basement. When a memory surfaced—the belt buckle scraping, the metallic taste—she shoved it down with such force that she felt dizzy. She told herself she could not handle what was there. If she opened the door, she would fall apart and never put herself back together. She became good at suppressing. But the fragments leaked through anyway: a clear image of the fluorescent light, then nothing; guilt so heavy it sat on her chest like a stone. She did not understand what she had done wrong—she had not given any names—but the guilt was there, hot and persistent, as if she had failed someone she could not name.

The congregation noticed. Preeti had stopped visiting the sick. She had stopped accepting invitations to dinner. She said she was tired, but the truth was that she no longer believed she was capable of doing the things that had once defined her. She watched herself from a distance, a woman who used to preach hope, and she saw no future at all. Only the same days ahead, each one requiring her to be hypervigilant, to taste metal in her mouth, to press down the guilt and the fragments and the fear that she would never be safe again. She came to therapy because her deacon—a kind, persistent woman—had found her crying in the church kitchen after a funeral reception, and would not let her deflect. Preeti sat in the waiting room with her hands folded, afraid of what talking would do, but also, somewhere beneath the hopelessness, hoping that maybe the pieces could be made to fit together without destroying her.
